## Course presentation

## Course content

The objective of the course is to introduce the field of *computational imaging* while developing practical skills.

The course covers the following themes:

- Principles of *computational imaging*
- State of the art of modern *computational imaging*
- In-depth analysis of *computational imaging* applications

## Assessment

| Component | Weight |
|---|---|
| Theoretical part (2 CC or oral exam) | 40% |
| TPs | 25% |
| Mini-project (report + presentation) | 35% |

Important points:

- The theoretical part is evaluated on the basis of 2 continuous tests **or** an oral exam

## Introduction to Computational Imaging

## Why “imaging”?

The term *imaging* is justified by the central importance of vision in human perception:

| Meaning | Share of information |
|---|---|
| **Sight** | **75%** |
| Hearing | 13% |
| Touch | 6% |
| Taste | 3% |
| Smell (Smell) | 3% |

> Approximately **75% of the information** that we perceive passes through the human visual channel.

## Why “computational”?

### Definition

**Computational imaging** is the process of indirectly forming images from measurements, using algorithms requiring a significant amount of computation.

Unlike traditional imaging, *computational imaging* systems involve **tight integration** between the capture system and the calculation.

The main objective of *computational imaging* is to **reconstruct human-recognizable images** from measured data, using advanced algorithms.

In contrast, traditional imaging aims to **process already recognizable images** to improve their quality or extract information.

---

### Traditional Imaging vs Computational Imaging

#### Traditional imagery

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Monde réel] --> B[Optique]
    B --> C[Image capturée]
    C --> D[Calcul]
    D --> E[Image améliorée]
```

- The optics capture something **close** to the final image
- The calculation **improves** mainly the captured image (e.g.: deblurring)

#### Computational Imaging

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Monde réel] --> B["Optique\ngénéralisée (?)"]
    B --> C["Représentation\ncodée (?)"]
    C --> D["Calcul\ngénéralisé (?)"]
    D --> E["Image(s)\nfinale(s)"]
```

- **generalized optics** encodes the world in an intermediate representation
- The **generalized calculation** decodes this representation into one or more final images

---

### Components of Computational Imaging

*Computational imaging* is located at the intersection of three areas:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    subgraph Monde_physique["Monde physique/analogique"]
        M[Mathématiques]
        P[Physique]
    end
    subgraph Monde_numerique["Monde numérique"]
        C[Calcul / Computation]
    end
    CI["⬤ Computational Imaging"]
    M --- CI
    P --- CI
    C --- CI
```

Two essential characteristics:

- Access to the **physical/analog** and **digital** worlds
- Consideration of imagery as an **integrated capture and inference model**

---

### Positioning in optical physics

*Computational imaging* is mainly at the level of **geometric optics**, enriched by modern signal processing:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    EM["Électromagnétisme\n(E&M)"]
    WO["Optique ondulatoire\n(Wave Optics)"]
    GO["Optique géométrique\n(Geometric Optics)"]
    SP["Traitement du signal moderne,\nOptimisation et IA"]

    EM --> WO --> GO
    GO <--> SP
```

Properties of light in geometric optics:

- Light modeled as **rays**
- Unit: **radiance** (spectral)
- Properties: wavelength, polarization, direction, etc.
- Wave optics is only briefly introduced

---

### General diagram of Computational Imaging

*Computational imaging* is based on two fundamental steps:

1. **Encode** the scene information optically
2. **Recover** information computationally

This implies:

- **new types of optics**
- **new sensors**
- **new lighting systems**
- **new algorithms**

#### Example: Computational Displays

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    CPU[Calcul] --> OE["Optique &\nÉlectronique"]
    OE --> HVS["Système visuel\nhumain"]
    HVS -.->|interaction| CPU
```

#### Example: Computational Imaging (camera)

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    O[Optique] --> S[Capteur]
    S --> C[Calcul]
```

## Biological example: the eye of the mantis shrimp

The mantis shrimp is a remarkable example of biological computational imaging.

Its compound eyes have extraordinary properties which perfectly illustrate the philosophy of *computational imaging*: a **deep integration** between the optical capture system and the neural processing of information.

## Areas of application

*Computational imaging* is applied in many areas:

- **Digital photography** — image processing, demosaicing, HDR
- **Autonomous vehicles** — cameras, LIDARs, radars
- **Endoscopy** — miniaturized medical imaging
- **Medical imaging** — CT, MRI, PET, 3D ultrasound
- **Astronomy** — telescopes, radio interferometry
- **Night / thermal vision** — infrared cameras
- **Connected glasses / AR/VR** — *computational displays*

## Motivating Examples

## Nanoscale microscopy

### STM and AFM: spin imaging at the atomic scale

Two compatible methods allow achieving atomic resolution for spin detection:

- **SP-STM** (*Spin-Polarised Scanning Tunneling Microscopy*) — local detection of a spin component of the tunneling current
- **nc-AFM** (*Non-Contact Atom Force Microscopy*) — detection of local forces linked to magnetic exchange

### Nanometric MRI

**MRFM** (*Magnetic Resonance Force Microscopy*) relies on mechanical force sensors to detect the weak magnetic signal of individual nuclear spins.

Three complementary approaches (measurement based on the magnetic field):

- **(a) MRFM** — nanomechanical resonator + nano-scale magnet → force on the spins of the sample (microstrip antenna for RF pulses)
- **(b) NV-NanoMRI** — electronic spin defect in diamond (NV center) a few nanometers from the surface
- **(c) ESR-STM** — tunneling current between a scanning tip and a conductive substrate

| Method | Range | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| MRFM | 100nm | 1nm |
| NV-NanoMRI | 10nm | 0.1nm |
| ESR-STM | 1nm | < 0.1 nm |

### Coherent X-ray imaging of magnetic systems

Coherent X-ray magnetic imaging is a **lens-free** approach to magnetic microscopy.

Strong points:

- Simultaneous access to **phase** and **absorption** contrasts specific to each element
- Spatial resolution limited by wavelength: **5 nm in 2D**, **10 nm in 3D**

Historical milestones:

- **2004** — Magnetic FTH
- **2011** — Magnetic Ptychography
- **2015** — Monitoring the dynamics of skyrmions
- **2017** — 3D spin texture mapping
- **2021** — Filming spin dynamics in femtoseconds
- **2023** — Capturing magnetic fluctuations
- *Future* — Imaging at natural scale, widespread application

## Astronomical applications

### Open questions: understanding the Universe

The big questions of modern cosmology require extremely powerful measuring instruments:

- Origin of the Universe and inflation
- Dark matter and dark energy
- Formation of galaxies and planets
- Large-scale cosmology

### The SKA network (*Square Kilometer Array*)

#### Acquisition sensors

**SKA1-Low** (Australia, Murchison):

- 131,072 low frequency antennas
- 512 stations of 256 dipoles each
- Frequencies: 50–350 MHz
- Baselines: 65 km

**SKA1-Mid** (South Africa, Karoo):

- 197 parabolic antennas ($133 \times 15\text{m} + 64 \times 13.5\text{m}$)
- Frequencies: 0.35–15.4 GHz
- Baselines: 150 km

#### Data volume generated

- Raw throughput: $\sim 2$ Pb/s (SKA1-Low), $\sim 9$ Tb/s (SKA1-Mid)
- After central processing: $\sim 7$ Tb/s → $\sim 5$ Tb/s
- Annual storage: **300 PB/year** per instrument
- Required computing power: **$\sim 130$ PFlops** per instrument
- Problem not in the acquisition, but in the processing of information!

## Medical imaging

### Classification of medical imaging methods

| Method | Information vector | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Ultrasound | High frequency pressure waves | Backscatter/Reflection Imaging |
| X-ray (projection) | Ionizing radiation | Transmission Imaging |
| CT/C-arm Computed Tomography | Ionizing radiation | Transmission Imaging |
| Nuclear imaging (SPECT, PET) | Ionizing radiation | Emission Imaging |
| MRI | Nuclear spin precession | Magnetic resonance imaging |

**General treatment pipeline:**

1. Acquisition of multiple 1D and 2D signals
2. Reconstruction of the 3D object

### Examples of medical images

- **3D ultrasound** — fetal visualization
- **Projected radiography** — X-ray transmission
- **CT (Computed Tomography)** — 3D reconstruction of the body
- **PET** (*Positron Emission Tomography*) — functional imaging

### MRI: advanced modalities

- **Structural MRI** — anatomy
- **MRA** (*MR Angiography*) — blood vessels
- **MRS** (*Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy*) — local chemical composition
- **fMRI** (*Functional MRI*) — brain activity
- **CDI** (*Current Density Imaging*) — mapping of brain currents

## Computational photography

### Imaging by mobile devices

Modern smartphones integrate several sensors and lenses to implement *computational photography* algorithms:

- Multi-sensor fusion
- HDR (*High Dynamic Range*)
- Night mode (*Night Mode*)
- Portrait with artificial background blur

### Multi-sensor / hyperspectral imaging

Cameras equipped with **multiple lenses** (e.g.: Light L16) allow multiple perspectives and wavelengths to be captured simultaneously.

## Automotive industry

### Autonomous vehicles

An autonomous vehicle integrates numerous *computational imaging* systems:

| Sensor | Role |
|---|---|
| **Cameras** | Detection of pedestrians, cyclists, traffic lights, free space |
| **LIDARs** | High precision laser sensors, detection of fixed and moving objects |
| **Long range radars** | Vehicle detection and speed measurement |
| **Short range radars** | Detection of obstacles around the vehicle |
| **Articulated radars** | Long-range moving vehicle detection |

### 3D imaging for autonomous vehicles

**LIDAR** (*Light Detection and Ranging*) is a key sensor:

- Example: Velodyne VLS-128
- Generates 3D point clouds in real time
- Allows 360° perception of the environment

## AI-based solutions

### Deep Optics

The concept of **Deep Optics** consists of **jointly optimizing** optical components and end-to-end image processing.

#### General principle

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    subgraph Physical["Couche physique"]
        L["Optique\n(lentille)"]
    end
    subgraph Digital["Couche numérique"]
        N["Réseau de neurones"]
    end
    Loss["Loss"]

    L --> N --> Loss
    Loss -.->|"rétropropagation\n(backpropagation)"| L
    Loss -.->|"rétropropagation"| N
```

#### Training phase (*Training*)

- **end-to-end optimization in simulation**
- The lens is modeled differently
- The network and optical parameters are co-optimized via a loss function (*loss*)

#### Inference phase (*Inference*)

- **Manufacturing** of the lens or other physical components obtained by optimization
- Execution of the digital network

**Two possible interpretations:**

- Optical encoder / electronic decoder system
- Hybrid optical-electronic neural network

## Analysis of works of art

### Examination of old paintings

Computational imaging allows **non-invasive** analysis of the internal structure of paintings.

### Structure of a painting (*stratigraphy*)

A painting is a multi-layer structure:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    V["Vernis / Glacis\n(Varnish/Glazes)"]
    P["Couches de peinture\n(Paint layers)"]
    S["Esquisse\n(Sketches)"]
    G["Couche de préparation\n(Ground Layer)"]
    C["Toile / Support\n(Canvas)"]
    V --> P --> S --> G --> C
```

### Traditional non-invasive imaging

Four complementary modalities for the same work (e.g.: *The Virgin of the Rocks* by Leonardo da Vinci):

| Modality | What we see |
|---|---|
| **Infrared** | Deep layers, sketches |
| **Visible** | Painting surface |
| **Ultraviolet** | Restorations, varnish |
| **X-rays** | General structure, dense layers |

### MA-XRF (*Macro X-Ray Fluorescence*)

**MA-XRF** is an elementary imaging technique based on X-ray fluorescence.

#### Physical principle

When a primary X-ray beam hits the sample:

1. Electrons are ejected from internal layers (K, L, M layer)
2. Outer shell electrons fill in the gaps
3. The released energy is emitted as **X-ray fluorescence radiation**
4. The characteristic energy identifies the **chemical element** present

#### Datacube MA-XRF

MA-XRF generates a 3D **data cube**:

- Dimensions $x, y$: spatial position on the painting
- Energy dimension: 0–40 keV, 4096 channels

This cube allows you to create **elemental distribution cards** (Calcium, Manganese, Iron, Copper, Mercury, Lead, etc.)

#### Deconvolution XRF

From the datacube, an **XRF deconvolution** algorithm extracts individual maps by chemical element.

Example (Van Gogh — *Sunflowers*):

- Copper card (Cu K-alpha)
- Zinc card
- Iron Card
- Lead Card

### Extraction of an underlying painting by ML

A machine learning approach allows **separating** visible paint from hidden (covered) paint from X images.

Example: Francisco de Goya — *Doña Isabel de Porcel* (NG1473, before 1805)

- **(a)** RGB image (visible paint)
- **(b)** X-ray image (mixture of the two paints)
- **Result**: separation into $\hat{x}_1$ (original painting) and $\hat{x}_2$ (underlying painting)

## Non-trivial applications

### Imaging outside line of sight (NLOS)

**NLOS** (*Non-Line-Of-Sight*) imaging makes it possible to **reconstruct hidden objects**, not directly visible to the camera.

#### Principle

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    L["Laser picoseconde\n(pulsé)"]
    M["Miroirs galvanométriques\n(2 axes)"]
    W["Mur (diffuseur)"]
    O["Objet caché\n(hidden object)"]
    D["Capteur SPAD"]

    L --> M --> W
    W -->|"lumière diffusée"| O
    O -->|"lumière réfléchie"| W
    W --> D
```

#### Time measurement mechanism

The depth is recovered thanks to the **time of flight** of the light:

- 1st bounce (laser → wall): reference measurement, e.g. $2.7\text{ ns}$ → $40\text{ cm}$
- 3rd bounce (wall → object → wall): contains information on the object, e.g. $4.3\text{ ns}$
- The difference $\Delta t = 4.3 - 2.7 = 1.6\text{ ns}$ corresponds to $\sim 24\text{ cm}$

#### Rebuild pipeline

1. Acquisition of **resolved temporal measurements** (3D datacube)
2. Application of a **3D reconstruction** algorithm (inversion of the problem)
3. Obtaining a **volumetric image** of the hidden object

#### Experimental results

- Real system: pulsed laser + SPAD sensor + galvo mirrors + occulter
- Hidden scene: statue + plant
- Result: identifiable 3D reconstruction of the scene behind the concealer
